extracted.intended_audience: investors, journalists, regulators, and the general public scrutinizing corporate governance and alleged misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: An investigative report cataloguing alleged corporate misconduct, regulatory violations, related-party dealings, and transparency failures at the Adani Group, with a long list of questions for the company and documentation of regulatory investigations. Intended to evaluate corporate governance, compliance, and investor risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty and transit-permit compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Any quantity (of ore) extracted and dispatched without paying royalty is illegal. The quantity of ore transported without transit permits (trip sheets, Form 31, Form 27) means non-payment of royalty and also theft of State property, hence has to be treated as illegal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance requires paying royalties and holding required transit permits (trip sheets, Form 31, Form 27); extracted/transported ore lacking these is to be treated as illegal and theft of state property (investigative finding; Pg.12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bribery and payments to officials
rubrics_metrics.description: The report states: “The Adani Enterprises has paid the bribes for getting undue favour for illegal exports.” It documents payments to port officials and others (per-ship bribes, port director payments, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of bribery includes transaction records showing payments to port department, Customs, Police, KSPCB, CRZ, Mines, local politicians and port staff. Recommended enforcement: criminal cases under the Prevention of Corruption Act and termination of government leases where bribery is shown (Pg.54–55, Pg.52).

rubrics_metrics.name: Related-party and beneficial-ownership disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous transactions involved entities later revealed to be connected to promoters (e.g., Vinod Adani-linked intermediaries); many deals were not disclosed as related-party transactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Firms must disclose related-party relationships and the beneficial owners of significant shareholders. Lack of disclosure (loans, asset transfers, investments by opaque offshore entities) is a red flag and may violate disclosure norms (many examples throughout, e.g., loans from Vinod Adani entities; related-party transfers to private Singaporean entity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate import valuation and invoice integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: DRI alleged Adani Power subsidiaries “grossly” over-valued import valuation of boilers, generators and turbines, falsified invoices and more than doubled declared import values to siphon funds abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Import declarations should match supplier/OEM invoices and be free of artificial over-valuation. Use of intermediary invoicing agents to overstate value indicates trade-based money laundering; auditors and customs should match customs declarations, supplier invoices, and payment flows (Pg.58, 67, 96).

rubrics_metrics.name: No use of intermediary/dummy agents to inflate value
rubrics_metrics.description: DRI called the Dubai-based entity “an intermediary dummy agent for invoice copying and value inflation.” Invoices routed through intermediaries in Dubai, Singapore, BVI, etc., were a central allegation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency about intermediaries, their beneficial owners, and the path of invoices/payments is required. Routing invoices through opaque intermediaries to inflate values or siphon funds is an indicium of fraud (Pg.32, Pg.96).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of source of funds for major shareholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Mauritius-based funds and other offshore entities collectively hold billions in Adani stock; the report repeatedly asks: 'What is the original source of funds for their investments in Adani companies?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public companies and regulators should be able to trace and disclose the original source of funds for large, concentrated shareholders; unexplained concentrated offshore holdings are risk indicators and may conceal related-party or illicit financing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure and explanation of large or inexplicable related-party loans
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include large loans from obscure or related-party entities (e.g., Krunal Trade & Investment lending INR 11.71 billion; Emerging Market Investment DMCC lent $1 billion) with no disclosure of related-party status or apparent business rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related-party loans must be disclosed, explained with clear underwriting and business rationale, and scrutinized for economic substance. Sudden large loans to near-zero-profit entities require explanation (examples and questions throughout).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of falsified laboratory/test reports for product quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The DRI alleged that laboratory test reports were falsified to show coal was of higher quality than reality to justify inflated valuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality tests must be conducted and reported honestly; falsified lab reports that materially affect price or tariffs are fraudulent and should be subject to forensic testing and regulatory action (Pg.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory/tariff transparency and no cost-padding via inflated imports
rubrics_metrics.description: Inflating equipment or coal import costs can raise energy tariffs (CERC calculates tariffs including return on capital). The report notes that if costs were inflated, consumers could pay more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tariff-setting authorities must verify claimed capital costs and inspect procurement valuation. Pass-through of inflated costs to consumers should be prevented by independent verification of import valuations and procurement records (Pg.10,15,17,20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely, impartial investigations and judicial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple investigations were stalled, shelved, or overturned; a former investigating judge resigned in protest. The report criticizes slow judicial movement and alleged governmental interference: “This Probe Has Been Shelved. This Has Been Done Under Pressure From The Government.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective accountability requires that investigations proceed without undue delay or political interference; overturning agency findings without transparent reasons undermines enforcement and public confidence (discussion on DRI shelved probe and appeals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of litigation/harassment tactics to silence critics
rubrics_metrics.description: The Adani Group allegedly used libel suits, gag orders, and other legal pressure to silence journalists, YouTubers, and protestors (e.g., attempted home raids, following protestors, defamation suits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect for free press and refraining from strategic lawsuits against public participation (SLAPPs) is a governance standard; aggressive legal harassment of critics is cited as evidence of attempts to suppress scrutiny and is an indicator of governance risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and transparency of corporate structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Adani's 7 listed entities have 578 subsidiaries and 6,025 related-party transactions in FY2022; the report notes investors prefer clean and simple corporate structures to avoid hidden conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overly complex, interlinked structures with extensive subsidiaries and frequent related-party transactions are red flags; companies should aim for clear, comprehensible ownership and transaction disclosures to reduce risk of hidden transfers or manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of roles/associations of key individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: The report asks for full details of Vinod Adani’s roles and the extent of his involvement, and seeks explanations for promotions and appointments of individuals with alleged prior accusations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should disclose historical roles, responsibilities, and relevant regulatory or criminal history of key individuals, particularly when those individuals have been implicated in prior investigations or arrests; lack of clarity suggests governance risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest in selection of advisors/underwriters
rubrics_metrics.description: Adani chose Monarch Networth Capital to run OFS offerings despite apparent close ties and prior SEBI sanctions; the report points to potential conflicts (small firm with promoter ties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection of brokers, underwriters, and advisors should be free from conflicts; use of firms with promoter links or prior sanctions for critical offerings demands scrutiny and disclosure of rationale and potential conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trading-pattern indicators of market manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Opacity of offshore holders, concentrated positions accounting for large delivery volumes, and extreme trading volumes suggest possible wash trading or manipulative activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators should evaluate concentrated offshore holdings, unusually high delivery volumes relative to float, and trading patterns consistent with wash trades or manipulative activity. Such patterns warrant forensic trading analysis and regulatory scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyst coverage and mutual-fund ownership as market-confidence signals
rubrics_metrics.description: The report documents thin sell-side coverage (many Adani stocks have 1–2 analysts) and that no domestic active mutual fund owns certain Adani stocks above 1% despite large AUM, implying avoidance by sophisticated investors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low analyst coverage and lack of significant holdings by major active funds can signal perceived governance or market-liquidity risk; these metrics are useful indicators of market confidence and investor willingness to hold positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to explain timing and purpose of asset transfers that avoid impairments
rubrics_metrics.description: The report highlights asset transfers from listed subsidiaries to private related parties that were then immediately written down, suggesting transfers pre-empted impairment recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transfers of assets that materially affect reported earnings or avoid impairments must be clearly disclosed with economic rationale; sudden transfers to related private entities followed by write-downs require explanation and may indicate earnings management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of participation in critical capital-raising events (OFS) and buyer identities
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2019 OFS deals for Adani Green required public-shareholder thresholds; the report asks what portion was sold to offshore entities and demands a full list of offshore participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies and regulators should disclose purchaser identities and the nature of participants in critical offerings (OFS) when such allocation affects public float or indicates concentration among opaque entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation and verification of corporate contractors / 'dummy firm' risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Large payments to contractors like PMC Projects (claimed ‘dummy firm’) with shared addresses and employees concurrently working across entities raise suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payments to contractors should be for bona fide services, with contractor capacity and independence verifiable. Shared addresses, overlapping personnel, and lack of independent operations suggest related-party or dummy firms and need disclosure and investigation.
